cim_eredeti: This Unstoppable Artificial Intelligence (AI) Stock Is Bucking the Tech Sell-Off, but Is It a Buy Right Now?
szoveg_eredeti:
Palo Alto Networks (NASDAQ:PANW) is the world's largest pure-play cybersecurity company. Its stock has exploded higher by 97% so far in 2026 (as of the market close on Nov. 19), and it has continued to trade in the green over the past month despite a sharp decline in the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) and Nasdaq-100 indexes.

The company is experiencing a surge in demand for its portfolio of cybersecurity products, as enterprises try to protect their digital assets from a series of new threats posed by artificial intelligence (AI). Hackers are using AI to constantly probe for vulnerabilities in corporate defenses, but enterprises are also placing their valuable data at risk every time they deploy AI chatbots, agents, and other applications.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

But is this fresh wave of demand enough to drive further upside in Palo Alto stock? Here's what I think.

The traditional approach to cybersecurity is no longer sufficient. Enterprises can't piece together products from different vendors and hope to achieve adequate protection anymore, because they rarely work well together and can't stop modern threats in real time. That's why Palo Alto is focused on "platformization," which involves encouraging its customers to ditch other vendors and consolidate their cybersecurity spending into its product ecosystem alone.

With this strategy, enterprises will have a unified set of tools to identify their weak points, uncover threats in real time, protect their data when deploying AI internally, and stop cyberattacks in their tracks.

Cortex XSIAM is one of Palo Alto's most successful products for the AI era so far. It's an AI-powered security operations platform that automates threat detection and incident remediation processes, reducing the workload on human managers who are struggling to keep up with the sheer volume of incoming attacks. XSIAM reduces the average customer's incident response time to just 10 minutes, from days previously.

Then there is Palo Alto's Prisma AIRS platform, which keeps track of internal AI chatbots and agents, and continuously scans third-party AI models for vulnerabilities. It's effectively a gateway for all AI-related traffic, guarding the enterprise against malicious applications. Idira is an identity tool embedded directly into Prisma AIRS, and it manages permissions to ensure AI agents only have access to sensitive data when it is absolutely necessary.

Palo Alto generated $3.4 billion in total revenue during its fiscal 2027 first quarter (ended Oct. 31), a 39% increase from the year-ago period. That growth rate accelerated from 34% in the previous quarter three months earlier, so the company is carrying significant momentum right now.

Palo Alto had 2,670 platformed customers at the end of the quarter, representing an eye-popping 84% increase. Those customers had a net revenue retention rate of over 120%, meaning they increased their spending by at least 20% (on average) compared to the same time last year.

Platformized customers are the biggest buyers of Palo Alto's next-generation security (NGS) portfolio, which includes AI products like Cortex XSIAM and Prisma AIRS. Annual recurring revenue (ARR) from the NGS portfolio soared by 66% to $9.7 billion during the third quarter, with that growth rate accelerating from 63% in the previous quarter.

Following its incredible gain in 2026, Palo Alto stock is now trading at a price-to-sales (P/S) ratio of 23, which is more than twice its 10-year average of 10.8.

Palo Alto stock is also nearly 4 times as expensive as the Nasdaq-100 index, which has a P/S ratio of 5.9, so by all accounts, it appears somewhat overvalued. As a result, I think there is limited room for upside in the short term, particularly with the broader market experiencing a correction.

However, Palo Alto believes it can more than double its NGS ARR to $20 billion by fiscal 2030, and if we assume it achieves that goal, then its stock looks far more attractive on a forward basis.

Therefore, whether or not Palo Alto stock is still a buy following its recent upside depends on investors' time horizon. Those hoping for further gains over the next 12 months might be disappointed, whereas those who are willing to focus on a longer-term period of at least five years could do very well.
